nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the novel of the young woman's consciousness
literary_identity: Novelist; the author of Dusty Answer and The Weather in the Streets, and one of the finest English novelists of the 1930s.
biography: Born Rosamond Nina Lehmann at Bourne End, Buckinghamshire, on 3 February 1901; she read at Girton College, Cambridge, and published Dusty Answer in 1927, which made her famous. A Note in Music (1930), Invitation to the Waltz (1932), The Weather in the Streets (1936) and The Ballad and the Source (1944) followed. She died in London on 12 March 1990.
literary_profile: Rosamond Lehmann was one of the finest English novelists of the 1930s: Dusty Answer and Invitation to the Waltz made the novel of the young woman's consciousness, and The Weather in the Streets is one of the great English novels of sexual love and its aftermath.
stylistic_characteristics: The interior monologue of the young woman; the party and the dance as social drama; the sensuous, exact description; the dialogue half-heard; the elegy for the lost love.
intellectual_concerns: Sexuality, the new psychology; the woman question, married disability, and the New Woman; class, the servant problem, and the new democracy; the suburb, the villa, and the new domesticity.
historical_significance: Rosamond Lehmann was one of the finest English novelists of the 1930s: Dusty Answer and Invitation to the Waltz made the novel of the young woman's consciousness, and The Weather in the Streets is one of the great English novels of sexual love and its aftermath.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the dialogue novel and the family tyranny
literary_identity: Novelist; the most original English novelist of the period and the great chronicler of the Victorian family.
biography: Born Dame Ivy Compton-Burnett at Pinner on 5 June 1884; she published Dolores (1911) and then, after a long silence, Pastors and Masters (1925), which established her style. Brothers and Sisters (1929), A House and Its Head (1935), Parents and Children (1941) and some twenty novels followed; she was made a DBE in 1967 and died in London on 27 August 1969.
literary_profile: Ivy Compton-Burnett was the most original English novelist of the period: her novels consist almost entirely of dialogue, and their chronicle of the Victorian family — its tyrannies, its murders and its cruelties — made her the great anatomist of the English household and one of the most admired novelists of the century.
stylistic_characteristics: The novel composed almost entirely of dialogue; the family gathered at the table; the cruelty stated as courtesy; the murder in the schoolroom; the absolute refusal of description and of the interior life.
intellectual_concerns: Class, the servant problem, and the new democracy; the woman question, married disability, and the New Woman; education, the schools, and the cultivation of the self; the absurd, the void.
historical_significance: Ivy Compton-Burnett was the most original English novelist of the period: her novels consist almost entirely of dialogue, and their chronicle of the Victorian family — its tyrannies, its murders and its cruelties — made her the great anatomist of the English household.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the fantasy of the witch and the historical novel
literary_identity: Novelist, poet and musicologist; the author of Lolly Willowes and one of the most original English novelists of the century.
biography: Born Sylvia Nora Townsend Warner at Harpenden on 6 December 1893; she edited the ten-volume Tudor Church Music and published Lolly Willowes in 1926, followed by Mr Fortune's Maggot (1927), The True Heart (1929), Summer Will Show (1936) and After the Death of Don Juan (1938). She lived with the poet Valentine Ackland, wrote the Kingdoms of Elfin stories, and died at Maiden Newton, Dorset, on 1 May 1978.
literary_profile: Sylvia Townsend Warner wrote Lolly Willowes, one of the most original English novels of the century and the founding text of the modern feminist fantasy: her story of the spinster who becomes a witch made a permanent argument for the woman's freedom, and her historical novels and Elfin stories made her one of the great English fantasists.
stylistic_characteristics: The fantasy that begins as realism; the exact and sensuous description; the spinster and the devil; the historical past rendered in present detail; the dry, precise, unsentimental prose.
intellectual_concerns: The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman; the countryside, the vanishing rural world, and the motor road; myth, ritual, and the primitive imagination; art versus life, and the romance of the artist.
historical_significance: Sylvia Townsend Warner wrote Lolly Willowes, one of the most original English novels of the century and the founding text of the modern feminist fantasy: her story of the spinster who becomes a witch made a permanent argument for the woman's freedom.

literary_identity: Novelist and playwright; the author of Hangover Square and the great English novelist of the London pub.
biography: Born Patrick Hamilton at Hassocks, Sussex, on 17 March 1904; he published Monday Morning (1925), Craven House (1926), Rope (1929, play) and Gas Light (1938, play), and the trilogy Twenty Thousand Streets Under the Sky (1935). Hangover Square (1941), The Slaves of Solitude (1947) and The West Pier (1952) followed. He died in Sheringham, Norfolk, on 23 September 1962.

literary_identity: Novelist; the author of Miss Mole, one of the finest English provincial novels of the period.
biography: Born Emily Hilda Young at Whitley Bay, Northumberland, on 21 March 1880; she married a solicitor and lived in Bristol, publishing A Corn of Wheat (1910), Yonder (1912), The Misses Mallett (1922), William (1925) and Miss Mole (1930), which won the James Tait Black Memorial Prize. She died in London on 8 August 1949.

literary_identity: Novelist; the great English novelist of the ordinary middle-class marriage, rediscovered in the twentieth-first century.
biography: Born Dorothy Stirrup at Blackburn, Lancashire, on 26 February 1893; she read at Liverpool University and published Young Anne (1927), High Wages (1930), They Knew Mr Knight (1934) and Someone at a Distance (1953). Her novels of the ordinary middle-class household were bestsellers of the 1930s and 1940s and were reissued to great acclaim in the 2000s. She died at Blackburn on 14 September 1966.

stylistic_characteristics: The domestic detail of the middle-class household; the marriage under pressure; the plain, exact, unsentimental prose; the ordinary woman as heroine; the comedy and the cruelty of the family.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the lesbian novel and the obscenity trial
literary_identity: Novelist and poet; the author of The Well of Loneliness, the most important lesbian novel in English.
biography: Born Marguerite Radclyffe Hall at Bournemouth on 12 August 1880; she published The Forge (1924), Adam's Breed (1926, James Tait Black Prize) and The Well of Loneliness (1928), which was prosecuted for obscenity in a celebrated trial. She lived with Una Troubridge and died in London on 7 October 1943.

stylistic_characteristics: The full case history of the lesbian heroine; the plain, earnest, sympathetic prose; the argument by sympathetic portrait; the war service and the Paris salon; the final appeal to God and to justice.
intellectual_concerns: Sexuality, the new psychology; the woman question, married disability, and the New Woman; the First World War and the myth of sacrifice; art versus life, and the romance of the artist.

literary_identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the author of 'The Beckoning Fair One', the greatest English ghost story of the century.
biography: Born George Oliver Onions at Bradford on 13 November 1873; he studied art in London and Paris, worked as a commercial artist, and published The Compleat Bachelor (1901), Widdershins (1911) and some forty novels. He changed his name to George Oliver in 1918 and died in Aberystwyth on 9 April 1961.
